## What this course is
The foundations of statistics and machine learning: probability, estimation, regression, classification, decision-making under uncertainty, model selection, and deep learning.

The term is in two parts. Weeks 1 through 6 are lectures and self-check labs. Week 7 is a review lab and the in-person midterm with no AI assistant. From week 8 the class flips: studio in the room, and the rest of your time is the project.

The foundation phase is 50\%: labs 10 and midterm 40. The project phase is 50\%. Across the course that is 50\% Understanding, 40\% Judgment, and 10\% Preparation. Of the 40-point midterm, 25 are Understanding and 15 are Judgment. Of the project phase, 25 points are Understanding (the defense) and 25 are Judgment (studio pages and the presentation).

Understanding means explaining what a computation or model does, interpreting its output in context, applying the basic principles without an assistant, and explaining the analysis your team produced. It also means knowing the basic concepts and being able to apply them. A correct number by itself is not enough. Judgment means the problem you choose, the alternative you reject, the cost of being wrong, and what would change the recommendation. Preparation is the labs: submit them on time and the 10\% is yours. I do not mark them. The notebook auto-grades the computations so you can check yourself. The midterm is how I check that the work became yours.

Given that AI assistants can write the code, fit the models, make the plots, and draft the slides, I will not grade a take-home write-up, script, or report as a document.

## Using AI in this course
You are expected to use AI assistants. Getting results from one is fine. I will not grade a take-home write-up, script, or report. Self-check labs are Preparation: submit them on time for the 10\%. The notebook auto-grades so you can check the computations; I do not mark the lab. Everything else that counts is something I can still attach to you or your team: the studio page in weeks 8 through 14, the midterm, the recorded presentation, and the project defense.

The rules are short:

1. Use whatever tools you want. There is no approved list. The midterm is the exception: no AI assistant and no machine. Pen and paper, one double-sided cheat sheet. That exam is how I check that you can apply the basic principles and concepts on your own.
2. Disclose what you used and for what, in a short appendix on submitted work. No penalty attaches to the disclosure. A team that used an assistant for everything and can defend all of it gets full marks.
3. You are responsible for everything you submit, including the parts you did not write. If you cannot explain it, that is on you.

## Course tutor

The course tutor is an assistant configured for this course. It answers R questions directly, asks you a question back before explaining a concept, and will not answer "which model is better?" until the purpose of the analysis is clear. Set it up once in week 1, about ten minutes.

Download [tutor-instructions.md](files/600/tutor-instructions.md) and [course-context.md](files/600/course-context.md). Then load them in whichever assistant you use.

- Claude or ChatGPT, if your account has Projects: create a Project, paste `tutor-instructions.md` into the project instructions, and upload `course-context.md` as a project file. Use that project for the term.
- Assistants without Projects: start a new conversation, paste both files into the first message, and add the line "Use these as your instructions for this conversation." Use one conversation per week and paste the files again; long threads get worse.
- Cursor, Claude Code, or a similar coding tool: put `tutor-instructions.md` in your course folder and set it as the tool's instructions file so it applies when you work on course code.

These files are platform-neutral, although assistants vary in how reliably they follow them. If you prefer a different one, paste the same two files into it. You can edit the instructions; it is a text file.

## What you will be able to do by December

**By the midterm.**

- Apply and explain the basic principles of probability, estimation, regression, and classification to a new problem without an assistant, interpret the numbers in context, and say what changes if an assumption or condition changes.
- Diagnose a defective analysis from its output: name the defect, point at the evidence, and predict which way the corrected number moves.

**By the end of the project.**

- Choose, fit, and validate an appropriate model in R, using evidence not used to fit it. Compare it with a simpler or more complex alternative, and say why that choice, including the representation, serves the stated purpose.
- State what each kind of error costs, and set evaluation measures, thresholds, and loss functions accordingly rather than by default.
- Quantify uncertainty and say what it means for the decision at hand, rather than reporting an interval and moving on.
- Establish where data came from and whether it is what it claims to be, then judge whether it supports the proposed use, who is affected, how errors fall, and who is missing from it.
- Delegate analytical work to an AI assistant and stay accountable for it: decide what to hand over, verify what comes back, and explain work you did not write.
- Defend an analytical choice under live questioning, and change your mind out loud when the questioning is right.

## How a week works

Weeks 1 through 6. Before class, about 90 minutes on that week's module: read the notes, work the material, and submit the self-check lab. The lab is a short notebook with three or four auto-graded exercises and one written question. Ask the tutor anything you got stuck on. In class the block is lecture and worked examples. There is no studio and no project yet.

Week 7. The seventh lab is due before class. Class is the midterm: 2.5 hours, pen and paper.

Weeks 8 through 14. Outside class you work on the project. In class, studio then critique.

- Studio. I put up a problem on that week's topic. Your team works it with your assistants. I do not walk you through it. I move between teams. Week 11 you work on your own project.
- Critique, about half an hour. Spoken, in the room. One team presents. Another team critiques it using the same five questions on the rubric: what they did, what the number means, why it supports the claim, what alternative they rejected, and what would change the decision. I assign the pairings. Most weeks two pairs go, so over weeks 8 through 14 every team presents at least once and critiques at least once. This is not a peer grade; I score both sides.


## Grading

| Half | Component | Weight | Understanding | Judgment | Preparation |
|------|-----------|-------:|-------------:|---------:|------------:|
| Midterm | Self-check labs | 10 | 0 | 0 | 10 |
| Midterm | Midterm | 40 | 25 | 15 | 0 |
| Project | Studio pages | 10 | 0 | 10 | 0 |
| Project | Defense | 25 | 25 | 0 | 0 |
| Project | Project presentation | 15 | 0 | 15 | 0 |
|  | Total | 100 | 50 | 40 | 10 |

The same 0--3 scale is used on Understanding and Judgment.

<!-- Understanding. 3: accurate mechanism, interpretation in context, and a correct prediction if a condition changes. 2: correct explanation, incomplete or needing a prompt. 1: repeats steps or output without saying why they work. 0: wrong, contradicted by the evidence, or cannot explain the submitted work.

Judgment. 3: names the decision and the loss, compares alternatives, calibrates the claim, and responds to a challenge for a stated reason. 2: the choice is defensible, but alternatives or consequences are thin. 1: a preference without a comparison or a decision. 0: no decision, no rationale, or keeps defending a claim the evidence contradicts. -->

For critique, I use the same five questions throughout. 1. What did you do? 2. What does this number mean? 3. Why does it support your claim? 4. What reasonable alternative did you reject? 5. What evidence would make you change your decision? The first three are mostly understanding. The last two are mostly judgment. A polished answer to 1 that cannot reach 3 is not understanding. A sophisticated model with no answer to 4 is not judgment.

Self-check labs. Seven notebooks, one for each of weeks 1 through 7. Due before class. Credit for submission: turn it in and those points are yours. The notebook auto-grades the computations so you can see whether they work; I do not mark the lab. Lab 7 is a review of weeks 1 through 6, due before the midterm.

Midterm. Week 7, the whole class, 2.5 hours, pen and paper. One double-sided cheat sheet. No AI assistant and no machine. I will post a problem bank. This is 40\% of the course: 25 Understanding, 15 Judgment.

<!-- Studio page. On each of the 7 studio weeks (8 through 14), one page before you leave. It is your team's write-up of that week's studio work, not the oral critique and not the project decision log. In this order: the decision; the finding; the evidence; the alternative you rejected; the strongest check that could have failed; what would change the decision. -->

Defense. Eleven minutes per team, Wednesday 9 December, 7:30 to 10:15 pm. Slots posted in week 13, two minutes between teams. Each of you gets two short questions, including about work you did not personally build: one explanation or counterfactual from the project, and one from the common foundations, not only from your team's chosen model. 

Project presentation. Teams of 3 to 4, locked in week 8, after the midterm. A five-minute recorded presentation due week 14 on Canvas. You watch two assigned teams and, on Canvas the same week, name the weakest claim you saw. That response has no separate points; it is required with the video. Code, plots, and analysis sit behind the talk; they are not a separate submission.

The proposal (week 9: a real decision, a stated loss, and a check on where the data came from), the mid-build in studio (week 11), and the decision log (submitted with the presentation in week 14) are required. I comment on them; they have no separate points. I will not assign the 15 presentation points until they are in. They supply evidence and material for the presentation and the defense.

If the team is not working, tell me by week 11. After that we can reduce your individual scope or reassign you. Waiting until the defense is too late. I will not ask the team to grade each other.

Scores of each component are normalized to be out of 100. Grades will be posted on [Canvas](https://canvas.gmu.edu). This course uses Mason's graduate regular scale: A\+, A, A\-, B\+, B, B\-, C, F. Cut-offs: 97 (A\+), 93 (A), 90 (A\-), 87 (B+), 82 (B), 79 (B\-), 70 (C). Below 70 is F.

## Computing
All work is in R. Install R and the Jupyter R kernel in week 1. Module 6 notes include some Python illustrations; you do not need Python for labs, studio, or the project.

Mason requires every course to make available the [Common Course Policies](https://stearnscenter.gmu.edu/home/gmu-common-course-policies/) (August 2026). They cover academic standards, accommodations for students with disabilities, FERPA and the use of Mason email, and Title IX. That addendum is part of this syllabus. Confidential options are listed there.

## What to do in week 1
Install R and the Jupyter R kernel. Set up the course tutor (see [Course tutor](#course-tutor)). Start noticing datasets you have access to through work, research, or an organisation you are part of. The strongest projects use data the team had to negotiate for or assemble. The weakest use a clean file downloaded from a competition site. Teams form in week 8 and you will choose a dataset then; it is much easier if you start looking now.

## Two things worth saying plainly
The most uncomfortable part of this course is being asked "why?" and not having an answer, in a room, out loud, while people wait. That happens to everyone here, including me. The ungraded practice in week 8 is there so the first time is not the graded defense.

You will encounter AI-produced work you do not initially understand. Your responsibility is to interrogate it before submitting and defending it. I would rather that happen here than at work.
